title: What is a cursor, when is it used (row-by-row processing when a set-based query cannot express the logic), and why is it usually a last resort (slow vs set-based operations, holds resources/locks)?
shortTitle: Cursors: What They Are, When to Use Them, and Why They Are a Last Resort

s1_definition.oneliner: A cursor processes query rows one at a time in a loop; use it only when set-based SQL genuinely cannot express the logic, because it is slow and holds resources and locks.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Row-by-row processing** – a cursor lets procedural code traverse query results one row at a time: declare, open, fetch in a loop, close.
- **Opposite of set-based** – SQL's natural model operates on entire sets at once; cursors are inherently iterative.
- **Last resort** – cursors are far slower than set-based statements, hold memory and server state, and can keep locks open for the entire loop.
- **Legitimate uses** – routing each row to a different procedure, sequential calculations that window functions cannot express, per-row side effects.
- **Senior rule** – think in sets, not loops; reach for a cursor only when per-row logic truly cannot be a set operation.
s1_definition.analogy: A set-based query is like telling the whole room at National Bank of India "everyone with a balance over ten thousand, step forward" and it happens at once. A cursor is like walking down a line of customers one by one, dealing with each individually. For most tasks the "all at once" command is dramatically faster; the one-by-one walk is only needed when each customer's handling truly depends on something you can only decide as you go.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Set-Based (preferred)              Cursor (last resort)
  ─────────────────────              ────────────────────
  UPDATE accounts                    DECLARE cur CURSOR
  SET balance = balance * 1.04       OPEN cur
  WHERE type = 'SAVINGS';            LOOP
                                       FETCH cur INTO row
  ┌─────────────┐                      process(row)
  │ Engine       │                   END LOOP
  │ optimizes    │                   CLOSE cur
  │ bulk         │
  │ execution    │                   ┌─────────────┐
  │ ~2 seconds   │                   │ Per-fetch    │
  └─────────────┘                   │ overhead     │
                                     │ ~120 seconds │
                                     │ Holds locks  │
                                     └─────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A cursor is a database object that lets procedural code walk through a query's result rows one at a time. This is inherently iterative, the opposite of SQL's natural set-based model where one statement operates on an entire set and the optimizer picks the most efficient plan.

A cursor is legitimately needed only when the logic is genuinely row-dependent and cannot be expressed as a single set operation: routing each row to a different procedure, a sequential calculation that even window functions cannot capture, or per-row side effects. Even many of these can now be rewritten with CASE expressions, window functions, or recursive CTEs.

Cursors are usually a last resort because they pay per-fetch overhead for every row, hold memory and server state for the entire loop, and can keep row locks for the whole duration. At the National Bank of India a junior wrote a cursor to apply month-end interest account by account, which locked rows and ran for minutes, when the correct solution was a single set-based UPDATE that produced the identical result in seconds.

The senior guidance is to default to set-based SQL. When forced to use a cursor, keep the result small, use a read-only forward-only cursor, fetch in batches, and keep the transaction short.

Remember one sentence: think in sets, not loops: a cursor processes rows one at a time and is a slow, resource-holding last resort.

---

keyPoints: A cursor traverses query results one row at a time: declare, open, fetch in a loop, close.
Cursors are inherently iterative and far slower than set-based SQL that the engine optimizes in bulk.
An open cursor holds memory, server state, and can keep row locks for the entire loop duration.
Legitimate uses include per-row routing, sequential calculations, and per-row side effects that cannot be set operations.
Many cursor patterns are replaceable with CASE expressions, window functions, recursive CTEs, or MERGE.
When a cursor is unavoidable, use read-only forward-only, fetch in batches, and keep the transaction short.
The senior principle: think in sets, not loops.
